From first principles

Full course

Fifty lessons that assume nothing. Every concept is built up from the one before, with a runnable program and an exercise at each step.

  • 50 lessons
  • New to Rust, or new to systems programming.
  • Runs real rustc — no install
Start lesson 1 Open in the app
01

Foundations

Your first program, printing and formatting, bindings, mutability, the scalar types, and functions.

  1. Hello, world! The smallest complete Rust program, and what each piece is doing.
  2. Printing and formatting Positional and named arguments, Debug vs Display, padding, precision, and the other print macros.
  3. Variables and mutability Why bindings are immutable by default, what mut really changes, and how type inference works.
  4. Shadowing and constants Rebinding a name to a new value — even a new type — and the two kinds of compile-time constant.
  5. Scalar types Integers, floats, bool, char — plus overflow, integer division and the casting rules.
  6. Functions, expressions and statements Declaring functions, the difference between an expression and a statement, and why most Rust bodies have no return.
02

Compound data & control flow

Tuples, arrays and slices, then if/loop/while/for and your first look at match.

  1. Tuples Fixed-size, mixed-type groupings — and destructuring, which you will use everywhere.
  2. Arrays and slices Fixed-length arrays on the stack, borrowed views into them, and bounds checking.
  3. if, else and conditional expressions Conditions must be bools, and if produces a value you can bind.
  4. loop, while and for Three loops, breaking with a value, and labelled loops for breaking out of nesting.
  5. match Rust's pattern-matching conditional, and the exhaustiveness check that makes it safe.
  6. String and &str The two string types, why there are two, and how to move between them.
03

Ownership & borrowing

The idea that makes Rust Rust: moves, copies, references, the borrow rules, and why dangling pointers cannot happen.

  1. Ownership Every value has exactly one owner, and memory is freed when that owner goes out of scope.
  2. Move, Clone and Copy Why integers behave differently from Strings, and what clone() actually costs.
  3. References and borrowing Using a value without taking ownership of it — the everyday alternative to moving and cloning.
  4. Mutable references & the borrow rules One writer or many readers, never both — and the data races that rule eliminates.
  5. Why dangling references cannot happen The borrow checker's other job: making sure no reference outlives the value it points to.
04

Structs, enums & pattern matching

Modelling your own data: structs and methods, enums and Option, and patterns in depth.

  1. Structs Named fields, tuple structs, unit structs, and the update syntax.
  2. Methods and associated functions impl blocks, the three forms of self, and the constructor convention.
  3. Enums Types that are exactly one of several shapes — and why they are more powerful than they look.
  4. Option — no null, ever How Rust represents absence, and the combinators that make it pleasant.
  5. Patterns in depth Destructuring everywhere: bindings, guards, @, nested patterns, refutability.
  6. if let, while let and let-else The lightweight alternatives to a full match, including the early-return idiom.
05

Collections & error handling

Vec, HashMap and UTF-8 strings, then Result, the ? operator and your own error types.

  1. Vec The growable array you will use more than any other collection.
  2. HashMap and friends Key-value storage, the entry API, and when to use the other maps.
  3. Strings and UTF-8 Why you cannot index a string, and how to iterate characters, bytes and graphemes.
  4. Result — errors as values Recoverable failure in the type system, and when panicking is the right answer instead.
  5. The ? operator Propagating errors in one character, and the From conversion that makes it work across error types.
  6. Designing your own error type An error enum that implements Display and Error, wraps causes, and plays nicely with ?.
06

Generics, traits & lifetimes

Writing code once for many types, defining shared behaviour, and naming the lifetimes the compiler cannot infer.

  1. Generics Type parameters, and why they cost nothing at runtime.
  2. Traits Defining shared behaviour, default methods, and the rule that keeps implementations unambiguous.
  3. Trait bounds and impl Trait Three ways to say 'any type that can do this', and which to reach for.
  4. Trait objects & dynamic dispatch Collections of different types behind one trait, and what it costs.
  5. Operator overloading & conversions Add, Index, PartialOrd, Display, From — making your types feel built in.
  6. Writing lifetimes out What 'a means, the elision rules that usually hide it, and 'static.
07

Closures, iterators & smart pointers

Functional Rust — closures and the iterator pipeline — then Box, Rc, RefCell, Deref and Drop.

  1. Closures Anonymous functions that capture their environment, and the three Fn traits.
  2. Iterators The Iterator trait, laziness, and the three ways to iterate a collection.
  3. The adapter toolbox map, filter, zip, flat_map, chunks, scan, peekable, windows — the chains you will write daily.
  4. Implementing Iterator Write next() once and inherit the whole adapter library.
  5. Box and recursive types The simplest smart pointer, and the only way to define a type that contains itself.
  6. Rc and RefCell Shared ownership, and moving the borrow check to runtime when the compiler cannot see your invariant.
  7. Deref and Drop The two traits that make smart pointers feel transparent and clean up after themselves.
08

Concurrency, async & beyond

Threads, channels and shared state; async/await; then modules, testing, macros and unsafe.

  1. Threads Spawning OS threads, joining them, and why move is almost always required.
  2. Channels Message passing with mpsc — the easiest concurrency to reason about.
  3. Arc and Mutex Shared mutable state across threads, with the lock built into the type.
  4. async / await Concurrency without threads — futures, the executor, and when async is the right tool.
  5. Modules, paths and visibility Organising code: mod, pub, use, and how a crate is laid out on disk.
  6. Testing Unit tests next to the code, assertions, expected panics, and fallible tests.
  7. Macros macro_rules! — writing code that writes code, and when not to.
  8. unsafe Rust The escape hatch: what it permits, what it does not, and how to contain it.

Every lesson here ships with a complete, editable program. Press Run and it is compiled and executed by a real Rust toolchain, so the errors you see are the errors you would get locally.
